Master’s thesis in Music & Musicology

The Use of SFX and VGM in Modern Era Video Games and Its Impact on The Gaming Experience

Elaborated byMohamed Hedi KECHICHE
Supervised byMyriem LAKHOUA
Academic year2025 – 2026

Game music and sound effects are one system, not two.

Video game music (VGM) has no visible source in the game world. Sound effects (SFX) do. Production, scholarship and criticism have kept them apart.

This thesis argues the split fails the player: each element produces effects that depend on, amplify, or cannot be separated from the other. Two case studies, a survey of 1,000 players, neuroscience, and a game I built test that claim.

Watch the two clouds. Amber is music, teal is effects. They begin apart and merge as the argument builds.

One question, three chapters, four kinds of evidence.

In a game the player is not a spectator but a co-author of the sound. So how does audio act on the person who both hears it and produces it through play?

Chapter 1: Framework

Ludomusicology, the history and typology of VGM and SFX, and the techniques of interactive audio.

Chapter 2: Two case studies

Assassin’s Creed, Ezio Trilogy (Kyd, 2009–2011) and Undertale (Fox, 2015), analysed as integrated audio systems.

Chapter 3: Impact, from four directions

A survey of 1,000 players. Neuroscience of cortisol and dopamine. The clinical U-shaped sequence. An original game, Hedi vs Evil.

Method: mainly analytical, supplemented by survey data and creative-practice research. The evidence converges; no single piece carries the claim alone.

A footstep can carry rhythm. A drone can carry harmony.

Ludomusicology studies sound in systems where the player’s actions reshape timing, repetition and structure. Adaptive music does this in two main ways: vertical layering adds or removes simultaneous layers, and horizontal resequencing switches between sections.

PadPulseArpeggio

From a beep to a language.

Sound effects began as functional indicators and became an expressive craft. Each hardware generation changed what a sound could be.

Pong. Analog circuits, short tones for contact, score, collision. Allan Alcorn added sound because a game ought to have some. The result: instant sonic confirmation of action, a convention that has barely changed.

NES. Five channels: two pulse, one triangle, one noise, one sample. Every effect had to be recognizable in a fraction of a second, what Karen Collins calls forced branding. In Castlevania’s “Poison Mind”, a fast arpeggio on one pulse channel does the work of full harmony.

SNES and Genesis. Eight channels with echo and reverb on one side, FM synthesis on the other: bright and punchy on Sega, warmer and richer on Nintendo. Effects became layered, and their expressive role grew.

CD-ROM. Storage for real performances and real ambience. Resident Evil used recorded footsteps and doors. Recorded sound carries a credibility synthesis lacks, and survival horror leaned on it.

Spatial audio. EAX, then binaural processing, faked distance, reverb and direction. In Metal Gear Solid 2, footsteps and alarms told you where enemies were: sound as a mechanic.

Technical necessity to expressive language. Today effects shape perception, rhythm, tension and spatial understanding in ways visuals cannot.

The sonic code

Contour carries the meaning, not the pitch. A rising slide reads as gain in any key.

A convention that stretches back through pinball and arcade electromechanics, and has survived forty years of hardware.

Assassin’s Creed: Ezio Trilogy, a score with two eras at once.

Ubisoft Montreal, 2009–2011: Assassin’s Creed II, Brotherhood, Revelations. Jesper Kyd recorded with live musicians, a Hollywood orchestra and choir at Capitol Studios.

His principle is dual register. Finger-style guitar, lute, harpsichord and solo voice sit beside synthesizers and electronic processing, so the music belongs to the story’s period and the player’s.

Because millions played it for dozens of hours, the score also transmits Dorian modal colour and the tarantella to people who never met Renaissance Italian music: cultural transmission, not decoration.

Jesper Kyd

Ezio as a lute player, AC II

Every theme grows from D Dorian.

The trilogy’s thematic material shares one modal centre. Because the open-world playlist can interrupt itself, any cue has to sit well beside any other.

Unison ostinato for finger-style guitar and synthesizer, with a piano processed toward a celesta. Kyd swaps the tarantella’s 6/8 strum for a single-line ostinato closer to minimalism, so the sound belongs to neither era.

A spatial leitmotif of mostly thirds and fourths for solo voice over a countermelody. Simple enough to be memorized, and it returns militarized in Brotherhood’s Rome.

A second D Dorian theme, for the brothel. It shares the Venice theme’s D–A fifth and a G–B♭ cadential gesture.

Built on the same intervals as the Venice and Forlì themes. Its first full statement comes in the execution scene, and from there it is Ezio’s sonic identity across three games.

A short, non-looping swell on the D Dorian centre, triggered when Ezio reaches a high point. It is compatible with any open-world cue, so it never clashes.

A timed-mission cue. A steady eighth-note pulse and syncopated sixteenths imitate a clock, so the music itself applies the pressure.

My transcriptions from Chapter 2.

Five and a half minutes, six scenes, and music enters in the fourth.

The execution of the Auditore family, AC II, Sequence 1, Memory 5, read with Julien’s functions of music. Click a scene, or play a synthesized sketch of its sound design.

A sketch of the design, not the game’s audio or Kyd’s themes.

The score’s power is in what surrounds it.

Four of Julien’s seven functions appear: decorative, phatic, conjunctive, melodramatic. Cinematic and ludic are absent, which fits a scene about grief.

The key beat fits none of them: the cut to silence at the drop. I propose a negative melodramatic function, where withholding sound does the emotional work a cue would. And a single moment can activate several functions at once, so the taxonomy works best as non-exclusive lenses.

A snare drum performs the phatic function that no cue does. “Ezio’s Family” hits hardest because of the emptiness before it.

A comment under footage of AC II with its SFX removed, which gathered over 3,100 likes. It lists sounds, not music.

Players list the effects they miss. No academic formulation of the SFX–VGM interlink says it more directly.

Undertale: the music takes part in the moral system.

Toby Fox wrote, programmed, designed and scored it alone over about two and a half years, after a 2013 Kickstarter. Released 15 September 2015, it has sold up to 7 million copies.

You can spare every enemy, kill them all, or land in between. Each route sounds different: the pacifist route is stable and characterful, the genocide route hears the same tracks slowed and destabilized, and sometimes the track is chosen by your moral record.

The score’s rule: tonal clarity and stable major harmony mean safety and compassion. Ambiguity and distortion mean violence.

Toby Fox

The introduction, in sepia browns

Silence first, then a cheerful lie.

The first moments of play have no sound at all. Chion would call it acousmatic deprivation: you become hyperaware of what remains, one golden flower in a dark room.

Then Flowey’s theme arrives in A♭ major over an Alberti bass, the innocent, domestic pattern of Classical keyboard writing. When the player dodges his “friendliness pellets”, the key falls a semitone to G major, a chromatic fall that signals betrayal. In the genocide route the same theme is played at a very low speed.

An illustration of the technique with an invented Alberti figure, not Fox’s music.

“Your Best Friend”, mm. 5–8, my transcription.

Music reveals what the story hasn’t said yet.

Asgore’s battle theme opens with a persistent sixteenth-note bass, and at measure 17 it quotes the B section of “Heartache”, Toriel’s combat theme. The score discloses their shared history while you are fighting one of them.

Likewise, “Small Shock”, two chords (C major ninth, B minor seventh), derives from the opening of “Snowdin Town”. Warm domesticity is attached, below notice, to a king who is kind and committed to murder.

“Heartache”, mm. 1–2 …

… quoted in “ASGORE”, mm. 17–18.

On the genocide route, the score forgets.

Three techniques degrade it. Tracks are slowed into dirges. Reward music is withdrawn: the shop theme never plays. And at the fight with Sans, the whole motivic architecture is replaced by “MEGALOVANIA”, the one track with no motifs from anything before it, and none passed on.

In a score built on motivic memory, a track with no past is a formal gesture: the sound of having no moral history. Finishing the route even alters the save data, so the same music weighs differently afterwards. Music becomes evidence.

“MEGALOVANIA”, mm. 9–10.

Tonality is the sound of salvation.

In the final battle, “Your Best Nightmare” alternates atonal breakcore with tonal reprieves, one for each human soul freed. When the player can fight back, “Finale” opens on solo piano and bursts into a forte in major at measure 17.

Harmony returns exactly when hope and agency return. Kyd’s Assassin’s Creed scores give historical and spatial immersion through modal language and place. Fox’s makes what you hear a consequence of what you chose.

“Finale”, mm. 1–4.

Audio also fails. The most common complaint was repetitive looping fatigue, at 38.4% of failure reports. Honest evidence has to include it.

The reported feelings are consistent with measurable biology.

Cortisol

Players with in-game music showed higher salivary cortisol at peak tension than players in silence (Peppler et al.). Silence in horror is audio work of the most precise kind.

Dopamine

Brain imaging shows reward-system release at musical peaks (Salimpoor et al., 2011) and during skilled play itself (Koepp et al.).

The U-shaped sequence

A clinical protocol that shapes tempo and density of music. One session reduced reported pain by 58.3% and anxiety by 74.3% in hospitalized patients.

Understanding comes from doing.

Music education has long held that learning is active, embodied and playful. Rousseau had children sing and move before notation. Dalcroze taught rhythm through the body. Orff placed structured play at the centre. Kodály began from the folk songs children already carried.

RousseauDalcrozeOrffKodály

Active listening as a condition of success

Identify an enemy approaching off-screen to survive. Time a press to a rhythmic cue. Follow an audio beacon to an object in a dark room. Practice under real urgency, with immediate feedback.

Same brain systems

Procedural learning and reward circuitry, trained by gaming, are the ones musical skill relies on. Games teach musical responsiveness without announcing themselves as teachers.

Next: Hedi vs Evil puts the claim into practice.

Hedi vs Evil: the argument, playable.

A first-person horror game I built in Unreal Engine 5 to make the thesis’s claims concrete. Deep red on black, with a 3D self-portrait modelled in Blender: a handmade work, not a commercial product.

The AI-generated ambience here is low and slow, with no melody. It isn’t meant to be noticed. It primes the body before anything frightening has happened.

Silence is not neutral. At the far end stands a figure. On reaching it, player control is disabled and three sounds fire, with delays calibrated to the startle response.

Against the U-shaped table: the quiet hallway is the plateau, and each sound is a step up. The laugh is diegetic, the stinger non-diegetic, and the scream sits in between, so at maximum fear the distinction collapses.

The Blueprint that disables control and sequences the audio.

The contrast room: brighter, warmer, and the AI ambience drops in volume. This is the descending arm of the U, built into the space without announcing itself.

The player engages the piano, and after a one-second “acoustic breath” a real recording of Beethoven’s Für Elise begins. The key animates, the door unlocks. They have made music and been rewarded for it: musical play in a horror engine.

The key can’t be found by a musical mechanic. The CRT’s audio grows louder as you near the desk. The player navigates by listening, and this is a sound effect doing the pedagogy, not music.

Try it: sweep the box to find a hidden spot by loudness alone.

Sound off. Turn it on, then move here.

What today’s AI tools struggle to carry.

I disclose it plainly: Suno generated the ambient textures. They took hours, not weeks, and they work, because they only need to sustain tension without a melodic foreground.

But Für Elise is a human recording. A model can match key, tempo and contour. In this comparison, it does not reproduce the micro-decisions of performing: attack timing, voicing, dynamics that follow the phrase, rhythm that bends to harmonic weight. Those encode understanding into the signal.

The spectrograms show it. Human audio is irregular and asymmetric. AI audio is flatter, with symmetric stereo and abrupt section changes. Nicholas Cook: the work lives in the performance, not the score.

Human (top), AI-generated (middle), and generative artefacts (bottom). Source cited in the thesis: BMAT / UPF-BMAT Chair on AI and Music.

What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t claim.

The survey

1,000 regular players recruited online, 71% at eight or more hours a week. It speaks for engaged players, and reports experience rather than measuring it.

The biology

Consistent with the testimony, and it shows the mechanisms are real. It does not show a jump scare works like a hospital session.

The case studies

Two games, 2009 and 2015, music-led. The SFX side rests on one scene and on my own game.

Hedi vs Evil

A proof of concept that makes the claims concrete. It has not been tested with players.

The AI comparison

Ambient generation against one human recording. A finding about current tools, not about AI in general.

Next

Player testing of the game, an SFX-centred case study, and recent spatial audio.

One sonic system, three contributions.

First, an integrated analysis of VGM and SFX as a single system, against the habit of treating them apart.

Second, a dialogue between musicological close reading and the psychophysiology and clinical music therapy that show its claims match measurable biology.

Third, Hedi vs Evil as creative-practice research: an original game that argues in playable form.

Game audio is not decoration. It is a physiologically active, pedagogically potent and irreducibly human system.

Thank you. Questions are welcome.

Who answered, and how.

Distributed digitally through Google Forms, via social media. 1,000 respondents, mostly 18 to 34, skewing to regular and heavy players: 71% play eight or more hours a week.

Why that is defensible: the testimony of people who play regularly is the relevant testimony for a thesis about the gaming experience. The scope is engaged players, and I say so.

Top genres: action/adventure 70.8%, open world 62.7%, RPG 57.0%, FPS 51.2%, horror 44.4%.

What each study supports, and what it doesn’t.

Cortisol (Peppler et al.)

With in-game music, higher salivary cortisol at peak tension than in silence. Supports: audio is an active physiological stressor.

Dopamine (Salimpoor et al., 2011; Koepp et al.)

Reward-system release at musical peaks and during skilled play. Supports: the reward response players describe has a neural basis.

U-shaped sequence

A clinical protocol: one session reduced reported pain by 58.3% and anxiety by 74.3% in hospitalized patients. Supports: shaping tempo and density of music reliably moves arousal.

The honest limit

These show the mechanisms are real and can be shaped. They do not show a two-second scare acts like a hospital session. Hedi vs Evil borrows the parameters; it does not replicate the protocol.

Two scores at opposite ends.

Assassin’s Creed: Ezio Trilogy

A large studio production: live orchestra, period instruments beside synthesizers, an open-world playlist. Sound gives place and history.

Undertale

One person wrote, programmed, designed and scored it. Sound is a consequence of what you chose.

“Modern era”

Read here as the period of recorded sound, adaptive music and spatial audio, from the CD-ROM era on. Recent spatial audio is a stated next step.

Likely questions, short answers.

Consistent with the testimony, not a confirmation of it. The clinical protocol shows the mechanism is real. It is an analogy for the scare, and I use it as one.

A proof of concept and creative-practice research. It makes the claims concrete and shows they can be built. It is not a test, and testing it with players is the next step.

In this comparison, with current tools, the performance details differ and the spectrograms show it. I make no claim about what future tools will do.

The claim is internal to Undertale’s score: within a score built on motivic memory, this track quotes nothing and passes nothing on. Check the exact wording against the thesis before the defense.
